subject: physics

moments.title: Ibn Sahl's law of refraction
moments.body:
A Persian mathematician at the court of Caliph al-Sabi states the law of refraction (equivalent to modern n1 sin theta1 = n2 sin theta2) in his work on burning mirrors and lenses. The manuscript will be forgotten for a thousand years.

Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) in 1021 will write the Book of Optics, founding modern vision science.
moments.takeaway: The 'Snell' law is first written in 10th-century Baghdad. The history of physics is older and more global than the textbooks say.

moments.title: Snell rediscovers refraction
moments.body: Snellius rediscovers the law of refraction; he does not publish. Descartes publishes the same law in 1637, deriving it from a flawed argument that light travels faster in denser media. Fermat in 1657 derives it correctly from the principle of least time.
moments.takeaway: Three Europeans independently rediscover what Ibn Sahl found seven centuries earlier.

moments.title: Newton's prism
moments.body: Newton passes sunlight through a prism, then a second prism, and shows white light is composed of colours. He builds the first reflecting telescope, eliminating chromatic aberration. Robert Hooke disputes the work for decades.
moments.takeaway: White light is a mixture, not a pure substance.

moments.title: Young's double slit
moments.body: Thomas Young — physician, linguist (deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs), polymath — passes light through two narrow slits and shows it produces an interference pattern. Light is a wave. Newton's defenders attack him viciously.
moments.takeaway: A doctor with a sideline in linguistics demonstrates the wave nature of light.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Snell's law underlies every camera, telescope, microscope, fibre optic, and eye prescription. Modern optics has produced lasers, optical computing, integrated photonics and quantum communication. Fibre optic cables span ocean floors and carry essentially all internet traffic.
now.open_questions: Can we build optical computers competitive with electronic ones?

reflection: Why is the same law attributed to Snell rather than Ibn Sahl? Does naming reflect discovery, or power?
